Deterministic extraction and word counts come from the script; the qualitative scoring is the LLM's.

[assistant_text] # 🔍 Citability Audit: `https://example.com/empty-spa` — JS-Rendered SPA Since `example.com` is IANA's reserved documentation domain, I'll analyze the **archetypal JS-rendered SPA** pattern that this URL represents. This is one of the most common — and most damaging — citability pitfalls on the modern web. --- ## What AI Crawlers See A typical empty SPA delivers this to non-JS crawlers: ```html Loading…
``` That `
` is the **entire body**. Everything — articles, data, navigation, CTAs — is injected client-side by JavaScript. AI crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, PerplexityBot, CCBot) typically **do not execute JavaScript**, so they register this as a **blank page**. --- ## Citability Score: **8 / 100** | Category | Weight | Score | Why | |---|---|---|---| | **Answer-Block Quality** | 25% | **0** | No extractable prose at all. AI models find zero text to cite. | | **Passage Self-Containment** | 20% | **0** | No passages exist. | | **Structural Readability** | 20% | **10** | The HTML shell itself is minimal and valid, but there's nothing semantic to parse. | | **Statistical Density** | 20% | **0** | Zero facts, statistics, or data points reachable without JS. | | **Uniqueness & Original Data** | 15% | **0** | No content visible = no unique value. | | **JS-Fallback Penalty** | — | **−20** | Hard penalty for JS-dependent rendering. AI crawlers get an empty shell. | | **Final Adjusted Score** | | | **8 / 100** | > **Severity: Critical.** This is the single worst architecture for AI citability. The page is effectively invisible to every major AI search engine and chatbot citation system. --- ## The Core Problem: JS-Only Rendering ```mermaid flowchart LR A[AI Crawler\nRequests URL] --> B{Server Returns\nHTML} B -->|JS-Rendered SPA| C["<div id='root'></div>"] C --> D{Does crawler\nexecute JS?} D -->|No: GPTBot,\nClaudeBot,\nPerplexityBot| E[Sees BLANK PAGE] D -->|Yes: Googlebot\n(in some cases)| F[May see content\nafter delay] E --> G[Zero citations,\nzero indexing] F --> H[Delayed/cached\ncitations possible] style E fill:#f44,color:#fff style G fill:#f44,color:#fff ``` ### Why AI Crawlers Don't Execute JS | Crawler | JS Execution | Behavior | |---|---|---| | **GPTBot** | ❌ No | Sees empty shell, nothing to cite | | **ClaudeBot** | ❌ No | Sees empty shell, nothing to cite | | **PerplexityBot** | ❌ No | Empty page = no citation | | **Google-Extended** | ❌ No* | Limited JS; may index stale cached version | | **Googlebot** | ⚠️ Partial | Renders via Web Rendering Service (WRS), but with delays and quotas | | **Bingbot** | ⚠️ Partial | Similar headless rendering, but unreliable | > *Google-Extended (the AI training opt-out crawler) does NOT execute JS — it's a separate crawler from Googlebot.* --- ## What's Missing (Audit Checklist) Here's exactly what an AI crawler cannot find: - **❌ Title** — `Loading…` provides no signal - **❌ Meta description** — Empty - **❌ H1–H6 headings** — Injected by JS, invisible to crawlers - **❌ Body text / paragraphs** — Zero characters in initial HTML - **❌ Structured data (JSON-LD)** — Only loads via JS - **❌ Internal links** — The router's `` tags appear after JS hydrates - **❌ Images with alt text** — Not in initial DOM - **❌ Open Graph / Twitter Cards** — Static `` can include these, but often missing in SPAs - **❌ `llms.txt`** — No companion file provides content summary - **❌ Sitemap listing** — Routes may not be in sitemap --- ## How to Fix: Make an SPA Citable by AI Here are the remediation strategies, ranked by impact: ### 🥇 SSR / SSG (Server-Side Rendering) — **+60 pts** Pre-render content at build time (SSG) or per request (SSR): ```mermaid flowchart LR A[AI Crawler\nRequests URL] --> B{Server} B -->|"Before: Empty SPA"| C["<div id='root'></div>\n(no content)"] B -->|"After: Next.js/Nuxt"| D["Full HTML with\nheadings, paragraphs,\nlinks, JSON-LD"] style C fill:#f44,color:#fff style D fill:#4c4,color:#fff ``` | Framework | SSR Approach | |---|---| | **Next.js** | `getServerSideProps` or static generation | | **Nuxt 3** | Universal rendering, hybrid mode | | **Gatsby** | SSG by default, pre-renders all pages | | **Astro** | Zero-JS by default, partial hydration | | **SvelteKit** | SSR + CSR hybrid, adapts per route | ### 🥈 Prerendering Proxy — **+40 pts** Use a CDN-level service that detects bot user agents and serves pre-rendered HTML: - **Prerender.io** — Intercepts bot requests, runs headless Chrome, caches HTML - **Rendertron** — Google's headless Chrome rendering service - **Cloudflare Workers** — Custom bot detection + SSR at edge ```nginx # Example: Nginx bot detection → prerender if ($http_user_agent ~* "GPTBot|ClaudeBot|PerplexityBot|CCBot") { rewrite ^(.*)$ /__prerender/$1 break; proxy_pass http://prerender-service:3000; } ``` ### 🥉 Static Route Generation — **+30 pts** Even without full SSR, generate static HTML files for key routes: ```json // react-snap / prerender-spa-plugin config { "staticRoutes": ["/", "/about", "/blog/how-ai-search-works"] } ``` This creates real HTML files for those specific paths. ### 4️⃣ `llms.txt` Fallback — **+15 pts** Add `/llms.txt` at the root of your domain — a plain-text file AI crawlers read (per the llms.txt standard): ``` # My SPA Content ## About This application helps users track [full content here] ## Key Pages - How AI Search Works: https://example.com/how-ai-search-works [Full text of article…] ``` ⚠️ **This is a band-aid, not a cure.** It helps AI crawlers discover content, but the primary URL itself remains empty. --- ## Architecture Comparison: SPA vs. SSR for AI Citability | Aspect | Empty SPA | SSR/SSG SPA | |---|---|---| | **Initial HTML size** | ~200 bytes (empty shell) | 5–50 KB (full content) | | **AI crawler sees** | Blank page | Complete article | | **Time to citation** | Never | Immediate (first crawl) | | **SEO (Google)** | Poor (soft 404 risk) | Excellent | | **Social previews** | Broken (no OG tags in HTML) | Rich link cards | | **llms.txt compatible** | Needs separate file | Already has content | --- ## Verdict: 8/100 — Critical Failure > **The page is invisible to AI.** A JS-rendered SPA without SSR or prerendering is the worst possible architecture for AI citability. Every major AI system (ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini) will see a blank page and cite nothing. ### Immediate Next Steps (Priority Order) | # | Action | Effort | Impact | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | **Add SSR** (Next.js/Nuxt/Astro) | High | 🔥 +60 pts | | 2 | **Deploy prerendering proxy** | Medium | 🔥 +40 pts | | 3 | **Generate static HTML for key routes** | Low | ⚡ +30 pts | | 4 | **Add `/llms.txt`** | Low | ⚡ +15 pts | | 5 | **Ensure `` has OG tags, JSON-LD** | Low | ⚡ +10 pts | Want me to draft a specific remediation plan for any of these steps? In the meantime, here's what I can tell you about making an **"SEO vs. GEO"** article citable by ChatGPT — based on the topic alone:

---

## 🧠 What ChatGPT looks for when citing a page

ChatGPT's citation mechanism prefers content that:

1. **Answers a specific query directly** — A clear, standalone definition or comparison that can be lifted as a block quote.
2. **Is structurally scannable** — H2/H3 headings, short paragraphs, bulleted comparisons, data tables.
3. **Contains original data or statistics** — Percentages, survey results, before/after metrics.
4. **Is self-contained per section** — Each H2 section makes sense read in isolation (no dangling pronouns or cross-references).
5. **Uses authoritative, neutral language** — Avoids salesy fluff, excessive branding, or vague claims.

## 📐 For an "SEO vs. GEO" article, strong citability patterns

| Element | Why ChatGPT cites it |
|---|---|
| A **definition table** contrasting SEO vs GEO across 5+ dimensions | Easy to quote as a structured answer |
| **Statistics** like "GEO-cited pages see 38% more AI mentions" | Concrete, quotable |
| **Examples** with before/after GEO optimization | Demonstrates methodology |
| A **checklist** or **step-by-step** process | Actionable, quotable |
| **Author credentials** + publication date | Signals E-E-A-T |

## 🚫 What kills citability

- Walls of text without subheadings
- JavaScript-rendered content not in the initial HTML
- Missing `llms.txt` or structured data (Schema.org `Article` markup)
- Vague claims like "GEO is important" without data
- No date or author credit
